October retail sales beat across the board with the headline rising 0.21%, vs the 0.1% estimate, taking the year-over-year figure to the highest since October 2022, even though motor vehicle dealers fell 1.60% and took 0.30 percentage points off the total.

Sales excluding autos and gas rose 0.52% versus 0.3% expected. The control group, which feeds GDP, rose 0.58%, the most since August, versus 0.3%, taking the year-over-year to 5.62%, the best since October 2022. September’s control group gain was also revised up to 0.53% from 0.14%. 

▪️ Headline +0.21% after an upwardly revised +0.83% in September (first reported +0.77%), and up 6.82% year-over-year, the most since October 2022.
▪️ Ex-autos +0.63%. Ex-autos and gas +0.52%, with September revised to +0.49% from +0.25%.
▪️ Control group +0.58%, and up 5.62% year-over-year, the most since October 2022. October alone is running 5.94% annualized above the third-quarter average.
▪️ Autos −1.60%, the biggest drop since July.
▪️ Gasoline stations +1.52%, and up 30.34% year-over-year, the most since July 2022.
▪️ Eight of 13 categories rose (although electronics was up just 0.03%). Miscellaneous stores led at +4.71%, the most since December 2024. Health and personal care rose 1.48% and is now up year-over-year for the first time since December 2025. Online rose 1.24% and is up 11.76% year-over-year, the most since July 2022.
▪️ Furniture −2.25%, the biggest drop since September 2025.
▪️ Bars and restaurants +0.24%, the smallest gain since March but a ninth straight increase.
▪️ Adjusted for inflation, with consumer prices up 0.35%, real sales fell 0.14%, the first decline since July.

Autos dragged on the headline, but the GDP-relevant control group beat by the most in months and September was revised sharply higher.

ADP Weekly Hiring Jumps to Most Since September

ADP’s preliminary weekly hiring estimate (the NER Pulse) for the four weeks ending October 31st jumped to +95k (+23.75k/wk), the best since the four weeks ending September 26th.

▪️ The four weeks ending October 24th were revised down slightly to +77k from +79k.
▪️ The 4-week moving average rose for the first time in five weeks to +79.25k, the best since the four weeks ending October 17th.
▪️ The current pace works out to roughly +102.9k a month. That’s above the top of the St. Louis Fed’s 15k to 87k breakeven range and far above the Federal Reserve Board’s estimate of under 10k a month.

The early-October soft patch now looks like a pause rather than something more nefarious. The moving average should keep rising next week as long as the next print beats the +67k from the four weeks ending October 10th, which drops out of the average.

@C_Barraud’s Tuesday Morning Brief had a couple of posts on the recent troubles of Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness. The fund’s third-quarter 13F, filed yesterday, holds an important lesson for investors. Its thesis (bets on AI) didn’t sink it. The fund returned 439% through June on that thesis. What sank it was a capital structure that couldn’t survive a drawdown.

▪️ July was the real blowup, and leverage caused it. The fund reportedly ran about 4x leverage. At 4x, a 25% drop in your holdings wipes out 100% of your capital, and AI infrastructure stocks have fallen that much several times in this cycle. When they fell in July, the losses reportedly triggered margin calls, and the fund sold its entire stock book to Citadel. Its investor letter showed a 67% loss for the month, and Bloomberg put assets at about $10B afterward, down from about $45B at the start of July. Recovery math is brutal: a 67% loss needs a 203% gain just to break even.

▪️ The downside protection came off at the wrong time. As of March 31, the fund reported puts covering $8.5B of stock in Nvidia ($NVDA), Broadcom ($AVGO), Oracle ($ORCL), Advanced Micro Devices ($AMD) and a VanEck ETF. By June 30, those puts were down to $5M, just before the July selloff.

▪️ Adding to the damage was a separate bet against software. The fund was also reportedly short software stocks, and those rose in July while its AI holdings fell, so even the short bets lost money.

▪️ The rebuild was a more defined-risk bet, but it looks badly timed. As of September 30, two-thirds of the $1.58B public book (down 92% from $20.2B at June 30) was call options on Bloom Energy ($BE), Nebius ($NBIS), Sandisk ($SNDK) and a memory chip ETF. Through Monday those stocks are down 35% to 55% from quarter-end, and the fund’s biggest stock position, SharonAI ($SHAZ), is down 63%.

Note, though, this isn’t a second blowup despite headlines. The public book is a small slice of a roughly $10B fund that’s mostly private holdings, led by an Anthropic stake Bloomberg valued at about $5B. At Monday’s prices, the stock positions are down about $325M, a few percent of the fund. The calls can lose at most what was paid for them, which the filing doesn’t disclose. Unlike borrowed money, they can’t force a fire sale.

The takeaway isn’t to avoid leverage or options. The same 4x leverage produced the 439%. The takeaway is to size positions so a normal drawdown can’t force you out. Losing money you’ve set aside to put at risk is survivable. Being forced to sell at the bottom is what turns a drawdown into a permanent loss

BofA’s Michael Hartnett says fund managers are still bullish on macro and markets in the November Global Fund Manager Survey, “but euphoria on boom & AI over.” Investors cut their tech overweight to a net 12% from 37%, the biggest one-month cut since June 2006.

The AI worries are building:
▪ 52% now expect an AI hyperscaler to cut capex in the next six months, up from 30% in October.
▪ A record net 38% say companies are overinvesting.
▪ Long global semiconductors is still the most crowded trade at 39% (down from 45%).

But they're not bearish stocks overall. 

The equity overweight slipped to just a net 41% from 44%, and cash fell to 3.6% from 3.9%, still in BofA’s “sell” signal zone.

For tech bulls waiting on a better entry point: Hartnett notes the best ones have historically come when investors cut tech to an underweight, and at a net 12% overweight they’re not there yet.

“Fund managers just made their biggest cut to tech since 2006, per BofA, but they’re still a net 41% overweight stocks with cash at 3.6%.”

Nvidia ($NVDA) is one down week away from tying its longest weekly losing streak on record.

▪ Six straight down weeks through Friday cut the stock 30.4% from its October 2 close. Monday’s 4.1% drop to $156.14 has week seven started.

▪ The only other seven-week run since the 1999 IPO was June 6 to July 18, 2008, when NVDA fell 53.2%. It has never fallen eight weeks in a row.

▪ Six-week runs are slightly less rare: one in 2002 and two in 2012. 

▪ At −33.3% so far, it’s also the fourth-deepest of the 13 streaks of 5+ weeks, behind May–June 2002 (−56.1%), 2008 (−53.2%) and March–April 2002 (−37.1%).

▪ The stock is now about 35% ($2 trillion in market cap per the WSJ) below its October 6 record close of $239.24.

What NVDA did after the 12 prior streaks of 5+ weeks (measured from the last down week’s close):

▪ 4 weeks later: higher just 5 of 12 times, median −1.4%.

▪ 13 weeks later: also higher 5 of 12 times, median −6.3%.

▪ 52 weeks later: higher 9 of 12 times, median +30.4%.

And the deep streaks (30%+ declines) were lower 13 weeks later in 4 of 5 cases, including −34% after 2008 and −46% and −50% after the two 2002 runs. One for the bulls: the last streak, which ended in October 2022, was followed by a 305% gain over the next year as the AI trade took off.

So the end of a long losing streak hasn’t been much of a buy signal for NVDA. A payoff might come on a one-year view, and that depends on the fundamentals holding up. 

Data: Yahoo Finance weekly closes; streak counts and returns are via Claude.

Ahead of Nvidia ($NVDA) earnings Tuesday, the Commerce Department moved Monday on the China loophole J.P. Morgan’s Michael Cembalest flagged in Friday’s Eye on the Market (“The Icarus Files”).

The new rule takes effect in 90 days. It requires a license for chips going to overseas data centers that sell significant computing power to Chinese companies, and for advanced chip exports to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

Why it matters, per Cembalest’s numbers:

▪️ Remote access to US chips is the largest single source of China’s projected AI compute at the end of 2027 (32%), according to the Institute for Progress.
▪️ 75% of China’s overseas compute sits in Southeast Asia.
▪️ The share of Nvidia’s revenue billed to Singapore addresses rose from 8% to 22% after the Biden-era export controls, and Nvidia stopped breaking it out in July 2025.
▪️ The House passed the Remote Access Security Act 369–22, but the Senate never took it up. Cembalest wrote that China hawks “appear to have the upper hand right now in DC.” Three days later, Commerce acted on its own.

His point is that the leadership fight isn’t the main risk; Nvidia’s weakening moat is. Nvidia holds 39% of frontier labs’ future compute deals, down from its 80%+ market share in 2023–2025. One frontier lab now gets models running on AMD chips in three days instead of 6–12 months.

If the remote-access curbs work, Chinese labs have more reason to build their own chips, and https://t.co/n1ZNIXVuhx, DeepSeek and Meituan already train and run models on Huawei’s Ascend.

He still sees a long-term case at a 0.2x PEG and 32% below the high, but it rests on the business, not the CEO.

Nvidia fell 4.1% Monday to become the third-largest US company for the first time in 18 months. It’s now down more than $2T from its October high, per the WSJ. Options price an 8% move on Tuesday’s report.

Goldman’s Brian Garrett (via ZeroHedge from @dailychartbook’s nightly email) flagged coming into Monday that global vol-control funds were modeled to sell roughly $27B more of S&P 500 stocks over the next few sessions. Then came Monday’s nearly 2% drop, which will almost certainly boost that number.

Coming into the week, Tier1Alpha had noted the biggest day rolling out of the 1-month window this week was only a 1.2% decline. Monday’s drop should lift 1-month realized vol to about 22.5–23% and 3-month to around 15%. That’s roughly where Tier1Alpha projected 1-month vol for Friday if the S&P swung ±1% every day, and we got there in one session.

BofA’s flat-market base case had vol control buying about $11B this week, but its down-market case had it selling about $10B. Monday put us in the down column. Goldman’s chart has exposure still around $130B, against a ceiling near $175B. Past deleveragings bottomed near $40B (2020), $80B (2022) and $65B (2025).

The calendar works against a quick reset. The Nov. 5 drop of 4.4% doesn’t roll out of the 1-month window until Dec. 4, and Monday’s drop stays in it until mid-December. And that’s with Nvidia’s results on deck for Tuesday.

@C_Barraud’s Monday Morning Brief had a few posts on China's monthly economic data that missed across the board. While the consumer was weak, the bigger story was investment falling apart despite Beijing’s stimulus efforts.

The headline misses:
▪️ Retail sales rose just 0.4% from a year earlier (vs. 0.8% expected and 1.1% in September), with autos (−21.4%) the biggest drag, per BofA.
▪️ Industrial output slowed to 4.8% (vs. 5.3% expected), its first slowdown in three months.
▪️ Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% year to date (vs. −7.0% expected and −7.2% through September).

That −8.1% is the weakest year-to-date reading since the 2020 Covid shutdown (−10.3% through April 2020). It’s also a sharp reversal: investment started 2026 up 1.8% and has slid almost every month since, after falling 3.8% in all of 2025.

By BofA’s calculation, single-month investment fell 16.1% from a year earlier in October, more than double September’s −7.2%, and that’s against an easy comparison (October 2025 was already down by double digits):
▪️ Infrastructure fell 17.6% (from −10.5%), after starting the year up 11.4%.
▪️ Property investment fell 33.2% (from −20.6%).
▪️ Manufacturing investment fell 9.3%.

BofA calls the infrastructure drop “especially disappointing,” given reports that the full RMB800B in policy financing tools had been deployed by the end of October. Its Beijing macro tour found limited support at the local level, and it warns growth could weaken further toward year-end if the current policy mix doesn’t stop the slide.

Nor is the PBOC rushing to help. Another headline in the brief says it withdrew medium-term funds, a warning sign for anyone betting on easing.

The one bright spot: urban unemployment edged down to 5.1% from 5.2%.

For U.S. markets, a weakening China is worth watching as a possible offset to the commodity-driven inflation the Fed is fighting.

▪️ U.S. stays overweight; Japan and Europe raised to overweight; EM stays equal weight.
▪️ End-2027 targets: S&P 500 8,700 (+15%), TOPIX 4,800 (+22%), MSCI Europe 3,030 (+15%), MSCI EM 1,760 (+13%).
▪️ Funded by cutting the rest of fixed income, commodities and cash; corporate credit raised to equal weight; likes gold.
▪️ Expects $1.7T of hyperscaler capex in 2027 and $1.8T in 2028, and says AI is broadening to adopters.

Wilson’s new 8,700 target (from 8,000) is 19x his 2028 EPS of $458. His EPS path is $369 / $420 / $458 for 2026–28 (+34% / +14% / +9%).

So the whole target raise has come from earnings. Since May Wilson has lifted his 2027 EPS 11% while cutting the multiple to 19x from about 20.5x. Notably his 14% 2027 growth is still below the 16.2% analysts expect (FactSet).

Note also the bank is calling for the 10-year Treasury rate to fall to 5.05% in 1H27 even with two more Fed rate hikes. “Our view dating back to late September has been that the correction associated with the mid cycle transition would conclude with the S&P 500 catching down to narrow breadth.
